Tell me about a serious conflict with somebody senior to you, and tell me how it ended.
In 2021 my uncle, who founded the company, wanted to bid for a large public hospital. I thought the payment terms were too risky for us, and we clashed about it for a week.
How did you tell him that you disagreed? He was the founder.
Not very well, at first. Our first conversation got heated. The second time I heard him out, and then I said: I see your point, but I am not sure our cash can carry a six-month delay.
And where did the two of you find common ground?
We both wanted the hospital. The sticking point was the risk, so I suggested that we bid as part of a consortium, with a bigger partner and a smaller stake.
Did he accept that?
He met me halfway. We won a third of the contract, and when the payments were late, the bigger partner carried the delay. On public contracts in general, we have agreed to disagree.

The conflict question is a trap for two kinds of candidates. The first kind has never had a conflict, or says so. Nobody believes that. The second kind tells me about a conflict he won, and describes the other person as an idiot. That candidate has just told me how he will talk about his classmates. What I want is a disagreement about something that mattered, with somebody you respected. I want to hear the words you actually used, because the words tell me whether you can disagree without making an enemy. And I want the ending, even if it was not a happy one. Sometimes the best answer is this one: we never agreed, but we found a way to work together anyway. That is exactly what a study group of forty executives from twelve countries will need from you.

The architect and I were at odds for most of the project. She wanted a glass facade on the west side of the building, and I knew the budget could not carry it. Our first two meetings got heated, and both times I stood my ground and won nothing. In the third meeting I changed one thing. I asked her to take me through the design from the beginning, and I did not interrupt her once. It took forty minutes. At the end I understood that the glass was not decoration. It was the only way to bring natural light into the patients’ rooms. So I stopped arguing about the facade and started arguing about the price. We found a supplier who could do it for twenty percent less, and she agreed to a simpler frame. Neither of us got what we wanted at the start. Both of us got something better.
